summary.title: Program-as-Weights: A Programming Paradigm for Fuzzy Functions

details: Many everyday "fuzzy" functions (log triage, JSON repair, intent ranking) resist symbolic coding and are outsourced to remote LLM APIs, sacrificing locality, reproducibility, and cost.

Program-as-Weights (PAW): a compiler-interpreter paradigm where a natural-language function specification is compiled once into a compact neural artifact that a small frozen interpreter LM executes locally per input.

The compiled program is hybrid: a discrete natural-language pseudo-program (paraphrase + I/O examples) prepended to the input, plus a continuous PEFT module (LoRA) generated in one forward pass by a trained hypernetwork-style compiler from its own prefix-position hidden states, mixed over shared learnable LoRA bases.
Training: only the PEFT compiler + mapper are trained, by backpropagating the target-output likelihood through the frozen interpreter (supervised, no RL).

10M (spec, input, output) triples generated with gpt-5.2 in two stages (specs, then 8 I/O pairs per spec); built over 29 thematic versions covering 800+ sub-categories (parsing, classification, format repair, NL-to-command, agentic tool use, HTML/web, safety).
80/10/10 split by specification so test specs are unseen; verified test set requires gpt-5.2 and gpt-5-mini to agree on the target.
Noise-perturbed test variants along 8 axes (typos, grammar, ambiguity, formatting, all-noise, terse, casual, paraphrase) at 3 intensities.

Pseudo compiler: off-the-shelf, never trained Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 with a task-rewriting prompt; LoRA compiler: same 4B checkpoint, fully fine-tuned, with T=64 learned prefix tokens and L depth-aligned hidden-state layers.

LoRA mapper: mean-pool over layers and prefix positions, residual MLP trunk, linear head producing mixing coefficients over N=64 shared bases per module type; rank r=64 on q/k/v/o/gate/up/down (~38.5M injected params per function).
Interpreters (frozen): Qwen3-0.6B (default), Qwen3.5-0.8B, GPT-2 124M; multimodal variant swaps only the compiler to Qwen3-VL-4B.
Training: 3 epochs over 10M examples, AdamW, lr 2e-5, effective batch 48, ~72h on 3 GPUs for the 0.6B run.
Direct prompting of Qwen3 0.6B/4B/8B/14B/32B, OLMo3-7B, gpt-oss-20B, plus gpt-5-mini and gpt-5.2 as ceilings.
Symbolic LM-to-code distillation (ALCHEmist), original numbers and a single-sample reimplementation.
Same-base no-compiler adaptation: full fine-tuning of the 0.6B interpreter and fixed per-task LoRAs at r=18/64/128.
Image tasks: AndesVL 0.6B, Qwen3-VL 2B/4B-Instruct.
FuzzyBench verified test set (exact match) plus WRENCH-style tasks (YouTube, SMS F1, Yelp, IMDB); image tasks: CoSyn Circuit/Chemical/Music, Im2SMILES-20K, Im2LaTeX-100K, TextVQA.
GGUF quantization sweep with llama.cpp and latency measurement on a MacBook M3 (Metal); Python/JS two-line API, hosted compile service, in-browser GPT-2 path via WebAssembly.
Five application case studies including a 10-PAW-function tool-calling pipeline on ToolCall-15.
PEFT form: prefix-tuning KV-cache mapper vs. text-to-LoRA at matched compute/program size.
LoRA mapper variants: per-position aggregation, per-layer bases, both, and LoRA+prefix combined.
Interpreter input: pseudo-program vs. raw spec (clean and heavy-typo); compiler input spec-only / pseudo-only / both; frozen vs. unfrozen compilers of 0.6B-32B (reported as inconclusive).

key_findings.finding: A 0.6B frozen interpreter running compiled PAW programs beats direct prompting of a 32B model on fuzzy-function tasks at roughly 50x less inference memory.
key_findings.evidence: 73.78% vs. 68.70% exact match on the verified FuzzyBench test set (Qwen3-0.6B PAW vs. Qwen3-32B prompting), ~1.2 GB vs. ~60 GB at bf16; the same 0.6B base prompted directly gets only 9.84%. gpt-oss-20B (85.45%) and API models (91.9-96.1%) remain higher.

key_findings.finding: The gain comes specifically from compiler-generated (per-specification) adapters rather than from LoRA capacity or fine-tuning on the same data.
key_findings.evidence: With the same 0.6B base, data and budget: fixed LoRA r=18/64/128 reach 42.4/52.1/51.6% and full fine-tuning 58.4%, versus 73.78% for PAW (+15.4 points over full FT, +21.7 over best fixed LoRA).

key_findings.finding: The discrete pseudo-program acts as a denoiser that makes PAW robust to noisy specifications.
key_findings.evidence: Accuracy drops at most 3.7% under combined heavy noise (0.6692 clean to 0.6326 all-noise heavy); ablating the pseudo-program in favor of the raw spec costs only 1.6 points on clean specs but 4.5 points on heavy-typo specs (0.6108 vs. 0.5662).

key_findings.finding: LoRA is the better program form than prefix-tuning for text, but the best PEFT is task-dependent, and simpler mapper designs beat more expressive ones.
key_findings.evidence: At matched compute: prefix-tuning 50.4% vs. LoRA 56.5% (r=18, matched size) and 65.7% (r=64). On long-form image-to-markup Im2LaTeX prefix-tuning wins (0.391 vs. 0.181), with a discrete-only ablation attributing the gap to pseudo-program examples consuming context. Mapper ablations: default mean-pool + shared bases 0.6223 vs. per-position 0.5598, per-layer bases 0.6028, LoRA+prefix 0.6033.

key_findings.finding: The abstraction extends to image-conditioned fuzzy functions by swapping only the compiler, and deploys cheaply on-device after quantization.
key_findings.evidence: With a Qwen3-VL-4B compiler and the unchanged 0.6B text interpreter, PAW beats up-to-4B VLM baselines on CoSyn diagram tasks (Circuit 0.274 vs. 0.196; Chemical 0.414 vs. 0.258; Music 0.552 vs. 0.470). Q6_K base + Q4_0 adapter (623 MB + 23 MB) is within noise of bf16 (0.6575 vs. 0.6580), Q4_K_M loses 1.3 points, and Q5_K_M runs at 31.6 tok/s with 0.48 s cold load on a MacBook M3.
